approachQuestion.prompt:
Schedule the most meetings

Select the largest number of nonoverlapping appointments [start,end), where an appointment ending at t may be followed by one starting at t. Return the count only. 0≤n≤200000; start<end; times fit signed 32-bit. Examples: [[1,4],[2,3],[3,5],[5,8]]→3; []→0.

Do not modify either input. Values are opaque comparison keys; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside the stated model. Choose the most efficient valid method that returns the required result for every allowed input.
constraints: Inputs are read-only and must remain unchanged.
Only comparison-based ordering is allowed; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside this problem model.

options.text: Sort by end time and greedily accept an appointment whenever its start is at least the last accepted end.
options.feedback: Earliest finish leaves the greatest remaining time for later appointments.

options.text: Sort by start and always accept the first appointment.
Sort by duration and accept each compatible appointment.
options.feedback: For [[2,4],[0,3],[3,6]], the shortest appointment [2,4] blocks both [0,3] and [3,6]; accepting those two yields 2 appointments.

options.text: Try each appointment as the first choice and recursively enumerate all compatible continuations.
options.feedback: This is correct but explores many schedules that the earliest-finish rule avoids.

feedback.reason: Choosing the compatible meeting with earliest finish leaves at least as much time for every later choice.
details: Sort appointments by end, greedily accept compatible entries, and update the last accepted end.

Choosing the compatible meeting with earliest finish leaves at least as much time for every later choice. Earliest start or shortest duration lacks that exchange guarantee. Respect the stated touching-endpoint compatibility rule.
“Sort by end time and greedily accept an appointment whenever its start is at least the last accepted end.”: Earliest finish leaves the greatest remaining time for later appointments.
“Sort by start and always accept the first appointment.”: For [[1,10],[2,3],[3,4]], this yields 1 rather than 2.
“Sort by duration and accept each compatible appointment.”: For [[2,4],[0,3],[3,6]], the shortest appointment [2,4] blocks both [0,3] and [3,6]; accepting those two yields 2 appointments.
“Try each appointment as the first choice and recursively enumerate all compatible continuations.”: This is correct but explores many schedules that the earliest-finish rule avoids.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed below, choose the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds. Count working copies, event/heap/visited storage and sort buffers; exclude the caller input and returned output. Comparisons and arithmetic take constant time; merge sort uses a linear buffer.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort by finish time, then make one compatibility scan.
details: The copied appointments are merge-sorted through logarithmically many levels with linear work per level. One forward acceptance test per appointment then adds O(n), leaving O(n log n) time. The copy and reusable merge buffer require O(n) auxiliary space; selecting only a count does not remove those working arrays.
